label_third_party_seals.detail: The gap between a certification and a marketing badge is entirely in the audit. Real programs publish their standard, so anyone can read exactly what was checked, and they send inspectors. The second half of reading a seal is scope: an organic seal covers inputs and practices and says nothing about welfare beyond a baseline, a welfare seal says nothing about pesticides, and a non-GMO seal addresses one issue only. Stacking seals on a package does not make it a better food, it makes it a food that paid for several audits. The ingredient panel still decides what the thing actually is. A badge a company created for its own products answers none of the three questions. USDA Organic, Real Organic Project, Certified Humane, Animal Welfare Approved, Global Animal Partnership and the Non-GMO Project all publish standards and use outside auditors. Real Organic Project sits on top of the organic seal and requires soil-grown crops and pastured animals. A farm that sells direct, where the grower answers questions about sprays, feed and pasture, reaches past what any seal audits. What no seal tells you is anything it never set out to measure.

label_artificial_color.detail:
The split is written into 21 CFR 101.22(k). Paragraph (k)(1) covers color additives subject to certification and requires each to be declared by the name in its own regulation, dropping the “FD&C” prefix but keeping “Lake” where it applies. Paragraph (k)(2) covers color additives not subject to certification and permits the collective terms instead, offering “Colored with ______” as the alternative that names the substance. Titanium dioxide is listed at 21 CFR 73.575, which sets the one percent ceiling and states that batches are exempt from certification.

So the generic phrase is a signal rather than a blank. Where a panel reads “artificial color” with no number beside it, the color is one federal rules did not require to be named, and the panel alone cannot say which.

A certified dye must be declared by its own name, so “Red 40” and “Blue 1” always appear as themselves. A color exempt from certification does not have to: federal labeling rules let it ride as “Artificial Color,” “Artificial Color Added” or “Color Added.” Titanium dioxide is the white pigment used for opacity in candy shells, frosting, chewing gum and creamy dressings, capped at one percent of the food by weight. A label may name it outright as “colored with titanium dioxide,” and nothing requires that. The EU removed it from food after a review by its food safety authority, and food makers there took it out. US rules still allow it. The plain move at the shelf is to skip a list carrying a generic color term and take one with no added color, or a color named from a food.
label_artificial_color.science: Certified dyes must be declared by name; colors exempt from certification may be declared as a group. Titanium dioxide is a white pigment exempt from certification. A label may name it outright, though nothing requires that. The EU removed it from food after a review by its food safety authority. US rules still allow it, under a group term if the maker chooses.

buying_tips: Almond drinks vary in added sugars, so the carton panel is the guide.
Look for unsweetened on the carton and no added vitamins or minerals on the list.
Whole dairy that suits you comes first. Almond milk is the fallback for a shopper skipping dairy.
Pick unsweetened over sweetened, vanilla or chocolate.
Some certified organic almond drinks still use carrageenan, a seaweed thickener; choose a carton with none listed.

almond_milk.why: Dairy comes first when it suits you. Almond milk is the fallback; almonds and water alone stay closest to the nut.
watch_out: Fortified almond milk comes second, since each added vitamin or mineral joins the list.
Gellan gum, guar gum or locust bean gum are added thickeners; pick almonds and water without them.
Skip an almond carton listing sunflower oil or canola oil.

buying_tips: Every addition is another ingredient; soybeans and water stays closest to the bean.
Look for unsweetened soy milk with no vitamins or minerals in the ingredient list.
Whole dairy that suits you comes first. Among plant drinks, nut or coconut milk ranks above soy.
Most U.S. soybeans are bioengineered, so choose certified organic first, with Non-GMO Project Verified a close second.
Carrageenan, a seaweed thickener, appears in some certified organic foods too; choose a soy milk with none listed.
A short-list unsweetened almond milk ranks above soy milk.

coconut_milk_beverage.decision: Canned whole coconut milk with no additives, over any carton.
buying_tips: The carton is coconut milk thinned with water, and gums like gellan thicken it back.
Look for coconut and water at the top, with no vitamins added below.
Reach for the can, not the aseptic carton: whole coconut milk with nothing added.
Read “beverage” in the name: coconut milk thinned with water.
Find it in the nondairy milk section, next to the soy milk.
Check for sugar and flavors on a sweetened carton.

buying_tips: Each type has its own card; the carton adds vitamins, pasture and filtering.
Choose the type first: milk, yogurt, cheese, butter, cream or a plant drink.
Across the case, whole and non-homogenized with no added vitamins ranks highest; raw from a farm tops each type.
Read the milk label for added vitamins A and D. Plain milk without them ranks higher.
Read a filtered milk panel for its protein and sugar lines.
Dairy cows can receive rBST, a synthetic growth hormone. Organic certification bars that treatment.
Choose certified organic dairy before a package stating “from cows not treated with rBST”. A package with neither ranks last, since rBST use need not be disclosed in the US.
